title: Two New Sea Spider Species Discovered in the Salish Sea — First in Nearly 100 Years
summary: If you ever imagined tiny hairy legs creeping up your body while swimming in the Salish Sea at night, you now have a real reason to shudder. Researchers at the University of British Columbia have identified two previously unknown species of sea spider, including one with long, curved spines on its legs and striking red eyes. The discovery marks the first new sea spider species formally described from the Salish Sea in nearly 100 years. The study, published in Organisms Diversity & Evolution, combines physical observations with genetic analysis. "That's largely because people don't know much about what species exist here and what their lifestyle is," said Toler-Scott, a researcher involved in the study. "In order to understand how marine invertebrates are being impacted by things like climate change and how we can better protect these key elements of the ecosystem, we have to be able to identify them." Sea spiders belong to an ancient lineage that arose roughly 500 million years ago. They are related to spiders, scorpions, and horseshoe crabs, but they remained entirely marine. Their appearance is strange even by arthropod standards. Some species can have as many as 12 legs, along with a sucking proboscis used for feeding. Their size varies dramatically, from less than a centimeter to more than 70 centimeters in Antarctica. Sea spiders also have unusual reproductive traits: they breathe directly through their skin, and males carry and raise the young. Researchers collected the new species between September 2023 and August 2024 during dives reaching depths of up to 18 meters. Specimens came from marine habitats around Quadra Island, Vancouver, Bamfield, and Victoria. One species was named Callipallene pilosuspedes because of the long, curved spines covering the lower portions of its legs. The name refers to the Latin words for "hairy feet." Its appearance is especially distinctive: red eyes and a short proboscis equipped with claws that help it grab food before biting. Despite its memorable appearance, the team found only a single specimen. The second newly described species, Tanystylum kiixin, takes its name from an ancient Indigenous village site near the location where specimens were first collected. Pronounced "kee-hin," the name refers to the sound of waves crashing at the base of the village site.
why_it_matters: Cataloguing what lives in the ocean is the first step in protecting it — without names and descriptions, scientists cannot tell whether a species is thriving or disappearing as the water warms and habitats change. The story also shows how much of Earth's biodiversity is still unknown, and how scientific naming can honour Indigenous places and languages rather than erase them.

background_read: Sea spiders are not true spiders at all: they belong to their own ancient group of marine arthropods, and their lineage has been around for roughly 500 million years — long before the dinosaurs existed.

The Salish Sea is the network of coastal waterways around Vancouver in Canada and Seattle in the United States, and it takes its name from the Coast Salish peoples who have lived along these shores for thousands of years. The study was led by researchers at the University of British Columbia (a large public research university in Vancouver) and published in Organisms Diversity & Evolution (a science journal where new species are formally named and described).

To name a species officially, scientists need both a physical specimen and a published description — which is why a single Callipallene pilosuspedes specimen still counts as a new species, even though the team found only one.

Scientists estimate that a very large share of ocean animals have never been identified, so discoveries like this are less about luck and more about how few people have looked. Species that are never named are hard to protect, because no one can tell whether their numbers are rising or falling.

perspectives.description: Researchers see this as proof that careful fieldwork plus genetic tools can still turn up unknown life in waters close to major cities. A new name means the species can now be monitored, studied, and included in conservation planning, and the Tanystylum kiixin name links the science to local Indigenous history.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — how solid is a one-specimen species?
perspectives.description: Describing a new species from a single individual raises questions: how variable is the species, and where exactly does it live? Critics of slow taxonomy also point out that formal naming takes years while habitat loss and warming move much faster, so some species may vanish before they are ever described.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical — a pattern of hidden diversity
perspectives.description: The Salish Sea is one of the better-studied coastal regions in the world, yet a century passed between descriptions of new sea spiders there. That fits a wider pattern: most marine species are thought to be undescribed, and odd groups like sea spiders — which breathe through their skin and have males carrying the young — remind scientists how much basic biology is still unknown.

The next step is more dives, DNA barcoding, and long-term monitoring to learn how these animals respond to warming water, pollution, and ocean acidity. If the new species are rare or locally restricted, they may need protection quickly, and their discovery could help justify stronger safeguards for Salish Sea habitats.
